title: Episode 208: The Greek Empire: Alexander the Great, the Phalanx, and the Hellenization of the East
description:
In the fourth century before Christ, the bronze belly and thighs of Nebuchadnezzar's prophetic statue exploded onto the world stage under a twenty-year-old military genius: Alexander the Great. Inheriting the revolutionary eighteen-foot sarissa phalanx and Companion cavalry from his father, Philip II of Macedon, and tutored in philosophy and science by Aristotle, Alexander launched an audacious crusade to conquer the Persian Empire. Shattering the armies of King Darius III at the Granicus and Issus, Alexander executed an engineering miracle at Island Tyre, constructing a half-mile causeway into the Mediterranean Sea. Marching down the Levantine coast toward Jerusalem, Jewish historian Flavius Josephus records that Alexander was met by High Priest Jaddua, who showed him the Book of Daniel foretelling a Greek king would overthrow Persia. Spared from destruction, Judea entered the dazzling, complex world of Hellenism. Discover the lightning rise and world-transforming legacy of Alexander the Great.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we enter the bronze era of the Greek Empire. In just twelve whirlwind years, a youthful king from Macedonia marched twenty-two thousand miles, defeated the mightiest empire on earth, and spread Greek language, culture, and philosophy from the Mediterranean to India. Here is George with the story of Alexander the Great, the siege of Tyre, and the meeting at Jerusalem.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: PHILIP II AND THE SARISSA PHALANX
Before Alexander could conquer the world, his father, King Philip II of Macedon, had to transform Macedonia from an impoverished, barbaric northern backwater into the supreme military superpower of Greece. Held hostage in Thebes as a youth, Philip studied the revolutionary tactics of Epaminondas. Ascending the throne in 359 BC, Philip reorganized the Macedonian army into a lethally disciplined military machine. He replaced the traditional eight-foot hoplite spear with the 'sarissa'—a colossal, two-handed pike eighteen to twenty-one feet long made of tough cornel wood with an iron point. Formed into dense blocks of sixteen ranks deep, the Macedonian phalanx presented an impenetrable forest of spear points that shattered conventional Greek infantry. Flanking the phalanx was the elite 'Companion Cavalry'—noble horsemen armed with xyston lances who delivered decisive hammer-and-anvil flanking charges. At the historic Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC, Philip crushed the combined forces of Athens and Thebes, uniting Greece under Macedonian hegemony, paving the way for an invasion of Persia before he was assassinated at his daughter's wedding in 336 BC. Philip of Macedon's military innovations fundamentally transformed Western warfare. The eighteen-foot sarissa required rigorous physical conditioning, turning rustic Macedonian peasants into the most formidable professional infantry force in the ancient world, supported by torsion catapults and mobile siege towers that redefined ancient siege tactics.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: ARISTOTLE'S PUPIL AND BUCEPHALUS
Ascending the throne at just twenty years old, Alexander III was a prodigy of intellect, romantic ambition, and athletic bravery. As a boy of twelve, he had astounded his father and the royal court by taming Bucephalus—a magnificent, vicious black warhorse that no adult groom could manage—recognizing that the beast was terrified of its own shadow, turning him into the sun and mounting him with calm authority. Philip wept with joy, declaring: 'My boy, seek a kingdom worthy of yourself, for Macedonia is too small for you.' For three years, Alexander was tutored in the idyllic school of Mieza by none other than Aristotle, who instructed the young prince in philosophy, rhetoric, geometry, zoology, and medicine. Alexander carried a copy of Homer's Iliad annotated by Aristotle wherever he marched, sleeping with it under his pillow alongside his dagger, modeling his personal identity on the warrior hero Achilles. In the spring of 334 BC, Alexander crossed the Hellespont into Asia with thirty-five thousand infantry and five thousand cavalry, casting his spear into the Asian soil and claiming the continent as spear-won land. Alexander's legendary bond with Bucephalus became a symbol of his charismatic mastery over men and beasts alike. Taming the warhorse by understanding its fear of its own shadow revealed the psychological insight that would distinguish Alexander's battlefield leadership. Aristotle's mentorship further instilled in him a profound curiosity for medicine, geography, and philosophy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE HAMMER OF GRANICUS AND ISSUS
Alexander's invasion of the Persian Empire unfolded with breathtaking speed. At the Granicus River, he charged into the swollen current at the head of his Companion cavalry, surviving a direct battle-axe blow to his helmet through the intervention of his bodyguard Cleitus the Black, routing the Persian satraps. At Gordium in central Anatolia, confronted with the legendary Gordian Knot of tangled cornel-bark rope that prophecy decreed could only be unfastened by the future ruler of Asia, Alexander severed the knot with a single stroke of his sword. In November 333 BC, at the Battle of Issus on the coastal plains of modern Turkey, Alexander faced King Darius III and a Persian host exceeding one hundred thousand men. Spotting Darius's royal chariot, Alexander led a furious, diagonal cavalry charge straight through the Persian lines. Terrified by the ferocity of the Macedonian charge, Darius panicked, abandoned his royal chariot, bow, and cloak, and fled on horseback, leaving his royal family, baggage train, and imperial prestige in Alexander's hands. Syria and the Levant lay open. The Battle of Issus in 333 BC proved the superiority of aggressive, combined-arms tactics over sheer numbers. Alexander's direct cavalry charge at Darius's personal chariot demonstrated his philosophy that victory belongs to those who strike the heart of the enemy, shattering the myth of Persian imperial invincibility.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE ENGINEERING MIRACLE AT ISLAND TYRE
While coastal cities opened their gates, the ancient Phoenician maritime metropolis of Tyre refused to submit. Situated on a rocky island half a mile off the coast of modern Lebanon, protected by massive stone walls soaring one hundred and fifty feet into the sea, Tyre was considered completely impregnable to land armies. Unwilling to leave a hostile fleet behind his lines, Alexander launched an unprecedented seven-month siege in 332 BC. Since he had no navy, Alexander ordered his soldiers to demolish the ruins of mainland Tyre, hauling millions of tons of stone, earth, and cedar logs into the Mediterranean to build a colossal mole—a causeway two hundred feet wide reaching all the way to the island fortress. When Tyrian fire ships set his wooden siege towers ablaze, Alexander mobilized allied Phoenician and Cypriot fleets, blockaded the harbors, and rolled catapults and battering rams right to the city walls. Breaching the defenses, the Macedonians stormed the island, slaughtering eight thousand defenders and selling thirty thousand citizens into slavery, demonstrating to the ancient world that no barrier on earth could halt Alexander's will. The engineering mole at Island Tyre remains a marvel of military history. Alexander's causeway permanently altered the geography of the Mediterranean coast, turning an offshore island into a peninsula that remains attached to mainland Lebanon to this day, requiring the felling of entire forests in Mount Lebanon.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MARCH TO JERUSALEM: JADDUA THE HIGH PRIEST
Following the brutal sack of Tyre and the siege of Gaza, Alexander marched his victorious army toward Jerusalem. The citizens of Judah, who had remained loyal to their Persian oaths, were gripped by terror, expecting the same merciless annihilation. Jewish historian Flavius Josephus records an astonishing historical encounter: High Priest Jaddua, warned by God in a night vision, ordered the city gates thrown wide open. Dressed in his sacred pontifical robes of blue and gold, wearing the golden plate inscribed with the sacred Name of God upon his mitre, Jaddua led a grand procession of white-robed priests and citizens out of the city to meet the conqueror at Mount Scopus. As Alexander approached with his generals, he halted his cavalry, dismounted, and walked forward alone, prostrating himself before the High Priest. When his general Parmenion asked why the conqueror of the world was worshiping a Hebrew priest, Alexander replied: 'I did not worship him, but the God who hath honored him with his priesthood; for I saw this very person in a dream in Macedonia, who exhorted me to cross over and conquer Persia.' Entering Jerusalem peacefully, Alexander offered sacrifices in the Temple, where Jaddua showed him the Book of Daniel, which foretold that a Greek prince would destroy the Persian Empire. Overjoyed, Alexander granted the Jews full religious liberty and tax exemptions in sabbatical years. The peaceful meeting between Alexander and High Priest Jaddua outside Jerusalem illustrates Alexander's respect for ancient religious traditions. By honoring the God of Jerusalem and offering sacrifices in the Temple, Alexander secured the unswerving loyalty of Judea, confirming his place in the historical prophecies of Daniel.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE FOUNDATION OF ALEXANDRIA AND SIWA
Alexander marched into Egypt, where the population welcomed him as a liberator from oppressive Persian rule. On the Mediterranean coast where the western delta meets Lake Mareotis, Alexander envisioned the intellectual and commercial capital of the Hellenistic world: Alexandria. Using barley meal to trace the grid layout of wide avenues, harbors, and public squares, Alexander founded a city that would house the famous Pharos Lighthouse—one of the Seven Wonders—and the Great Library of Alexandria, where the Hebrew scriptures would later be translated into Greek as the Septuagint. Alexander then undertook a perilous, three-hundred-mile trek across the blistering Libyan desert to the Siwa Oasis. Guided by desert ravens, Alexander consulted the famous Oracle of Ammon. The high priest addressed the young conqueror in Greek as the 'Son of Ammon'—interpreted by the Greeks as Zeus. Confirmed in his divine destiny, Alexander returned to Asia, prepared for the final apocalyptic showdown against the imperial forces of Darius III. The foundation of Alexandria in Egypt created the intellectual capital of the Hellenistic age. Its grid layout, designed by the architect Dinocrates, fostered a cosmopolitan metropolis where Greek philosophy, Egyptian science, and Jewish scripture flourished side by side, centered around the famous Great Library.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GLOBAL VISION OF HELLENISM
In October 331 BC, on the open plains of Gaugamela near modern Erbil in Iraq, Alexander fought his masterpiece battle against Darius's re-formed army of scythed chariots and war elephants. Executing a brilliant wedge maneuver with his cavalry, Alexander broke the Persian center, forcing Darius into final flight. Entering Babylon, Susa, and the ceremonial capital of Persepolis—which he burned in drunken retribution for the Persian burning of Athens—Alexander claimed the throne of Asia. He marched east across Central Asia, founding cities named Alexandria, crossing the Hindu Kush into India, and fighting the war elephants of King Porus at the Hydaspes River in 326 BC. Only when his exhausted soldiers mutinied at the Hyphasis River did Alexander turn back. In June 323 BC, in the royal palace of Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon, Alexander was stricken with violent fever and died at just thirty-two years of age. When his generals asked on his deathbed to whom he left his empire, Alexander whispered: 'To the strongest.' Though his empire fractured, Alexander's conquest seeded Greek language, art, and philosophy across the Near East, creating the universal cultural bridge that would carry the New Testament to the world. Alexander's campaigns spread the 'Koine' Greek dialect across the known world, creating a universal language of commerce, literature, and diplomacy that would later serve as the vehicle for the New Testament, unifying the Mediterranean basin under a common cultural umbrella.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Alexander conquered the known world with the spear, leaving behind an empire saturated in Greek culture. But upon his sudden death, his vast realms were torn apart by his warring generals. Next week, we continue our Greek saga with Episode 209: Antiochus Epiphanes, the Abomination of Desolation, and the Maccabean Revolt: the clash between Hellenism and Torah, the mad tyrant who sacrificed swine upon the altar, the guerrilla hammer of Judah Maccabee, the cleansing of the Temple, and the miracle of Hanukkah. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
